lesson.title: Average Atomic Mass: Why the Periodic Table Shows Decimals
lesson.summary: Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of all an element's naturally occurring isotopes, and it is the value printed on the periodic table.
lesson.body:
Look at any periodic table and you will notice that almost no element has a whole-number mass listed beneath its symbol. Chlorine shows 35.45, copper shows 63.55, boron shows 10.81. These are not the atomic mass of any single atom of that element. They are average atomic masses, weighted averages calculated across every naturally occurring isotope of that element, weighted by how abundant each isotope actually is in nature. This is the direct combination of two ideas already covered: isotopes, which explain why an element has multiple possible masses, and atomic mass, which gives the precise mass of each individual isotope.

The calculation itself is a weighted average, not a simple average. Each isotope's atomic mass is multiplied by its fractional natural abundance, expressed as a decimal, and the results are summed across all isotopes of that element. In formula form, average atomic mass equals the sum, for every isotope, of that isotope's atomic mass times its fractional abundance. An isotope that makes up 90 percent of natural samples pulls the average far closer to its own mass than an isotope making up only 10 percent, exactly the way weighted averages work in any other context, such as computing a course grade where exams count more than homework.

Chlorine provides a clean worked example. Chlorine has two stable natural isotopes: chlorine-35, with an atomic mass of 34.969 u and a natural abundance of 75.76 percent, and chlorine-37, with an atomic mass of 36.966 u and a natural abundance of 24.24 percent. Converting the percentages to decimals and multiplying: 0.7576 times 34.969 equals about 26.492 u, and 0.2424 times 36.966 equals about 8.961 u. Adding these two contributions together, 26.492 plus 8.961, gives 35.45 u, matching the average atomic mass printed on the periodic table for chlorine almost exactly.

A second worked example uses boron, which has two stable isotopes: boron-10, atomic mass 10.013 u, natural abundance 19.9 percent, and boron-11, atomic mass 11.009 u, natural abundance 80.1 percent. The calculation is 0.199 times 10.013, equal to about 1.993 u, plus 0.801 times 11.009, equal to about 8.818 u, giving a total of about 10.81 u, again matching the periodic table value for boron. Notice how strongly the more abundant isotope, boron-11 at 80.1 percent, pulls the average close to its own mass of 11.009, far more than the minority isotope does.

Average atomic mass is the quantity that makes the mole concept work in practice, because it is the number, in grams per mole, that tells chemists exactly how much a mole of any element's naturally occurring atoms actually weighs on a laboratory balance. It is also the quantity that mass spectrometry is built to measure experimentally, since a mass spectrometer directly detects both the mass and the relative abundance of each isotope present in a real sample, providing the raw data that average atomic mass calculations depend on.
